title: NVIDIA’s Groq 3 LPU Accelerators for Heterogeneous AI Compute at Hot Chips 2026
gist: Live from Hot Chips 2026: NVIDIA, having acquihired Groq's talent, is presenting Groq 3 LPUs as the dedicated low-latency decode layer (LPX racks) inside its Vera Rubin ecosystem — SRAM-heavy deterministic chips that push per-user token rates up to 5x beyond what Rubin GPUs alone deliver, with a 256-LPU rack packing 128GB SRAM, 40PB/s bandwidth, and 315 PFLOPS FP8.

insights.claim: NVIDIA does not currently make its own LPUs; the LPUs in Vera Rubin LPX racks are bought from Groq as part of a broader acquihire of the company, with the bulk of Groq's talent now at NVIDIA and in-house NVIDIA LPUs under development.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is absorbing rather than competing with the leading inference-ASIC challenger — neutralizes a rival architecture and closes NVIDIA's low-latency gap; watch for a fully in-house NVIDIA LPU generation.
insights.quote: come from Groq, whom NVIDIA is buying the chips from as part of a broader acquihire of the company

insights.claim: NVIDIA's coordinated push — first third-party LPX benchmarks released the day before Hot Chips, plus LPU promotion woven into both its Vera CPU and Rubin GPU talks — signals a deliberate campaign to position LPUs as a core pillar of the platform, not a side experiment.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Marketing cadence suggests LPX is a strategic product line NVIDIA intends to sell at scale; expect it in near-term datacenter roadmaps and revenue mix.
insights.quote: Yesterday NVIDIA released the first third-party benchmarks of an LPX rack, so the timing of that and this talk is not coincidental.

insights.claim: NVIDIA frames agentic AI as the most complex computing workload in history, using that framing to justify adding new hardware categories (LPUs) alongside GPUs and demanding much more total hardware.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Agentic workloads are the demand narrative underwriting continued AI capex growth — heterogeneous racks mean more silicon per deployment, not less.

themes.theme: LPU Role: Fixing the GPU Decode Weakness

insights.claim: GPUs are strong at prefill but only so-so at decode, and Rubin GPU throughput drops sharply when pushed toward higher per-user interactivity (lower token latency) — LPUs exist specifically to fill this weak spot in the Vera Rubin stack.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: An admission that GPUs alone can't serve low-latency inference economically — validates the inference-ASIC thesis (Groq, Cerebras) and explains why NVIDIA bought rather than dismissed it.
insights.quote: GPUs are great for pre-fill, and depending on how the design of the chip is optimized, so-so at decode.
insights.locator: Groq’s LPUs are designed to fill

insights.claim: In agentic AI serving, decode — driven by large context-token volumes — is the largest share of inference compute time, making it the highest-leverage stage to accelerate with specialized SRAM-based silicon.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Whoever owns decode economics owns agentic inference economics; SRAM-heavy architectures and HBM alternatives target exactly this stage.
insights.quote: Decode is the largest portion of the compute workload in term of the amount of time taken.
insights.locator: Agentic AI systems need a lot

insights.claim: Adding LPX racks to Vera Rubin extends NVIDIA's tokens/sec/watt-versus-tokens/sec/user pareto frontier by up to 5x at the highest per-user token rates, but total throughput efficiency falls the more work is offloaded to LPUs — GPUs remain most efficient when raw throughput at high latency is acceptable.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Latency and efficiency are now an explicit trade dial: premium low-latency inference tiers will carry higher silicon cost per token — pricing power for interactive agentic services.
insights.quote: GPUs are still the king of efficiency when total throughput is all that matters and high latencies are acceptable

insights.claim: A single LPX rack contains 256 Groq 3 LPUs, aggregating 128GB of SRAM, 40PB/s of SRAM bandwidth, and 315 PFLOPS of FP8 compute.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Hard spec baseline for comparing inference-ASIC racks; note SRAM-only capacity (128GB) constrains model size, implying multi-rack scaling or GPU pairing for frontier models.
insights.quote: there are 256 LPUs in a single LPX rack
insights.locator: Getting back to the physical world

insights.claim: One LPX rack decodes 11,000 tokens per second on a 31B-parameter model (Gemma 4), and Artificial Analysis third-party benchmarks showed 4x higher token output than the next-closest public competitor, which the author infers is a Cerebras CS-3.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: If the 4x-vs-Cerebras gap holds, NVIDIA's acquihired LPU line leapfrogs the main wafer-scale challenger in low-latency inference — direct competitive pressure on Cerebras.
insights.quote: The LPX rack offed a 4x higher token output rate than the next-closest public competitor, which NVIDIA doesn’t name but looks to be a Cerebas CS-3.
insights.locator: NVIDIA this week published third-party benchmarks

insights.claim: The Groq 3 LPU is fully deterministic with no branching, so instruction scheduling moves into the compiler/software, eliminating significant on-chip scheduling hardware and freeing die area for SRAM and compute.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Software-scheduled determinism is the core architectural moat vs GPUs — it trades flexibility for latency and area efficiency, a design point GPUs can't easily copy.
insights.quote: This is a fully deterministic chip. There is no branching or other sources of non-determinism.

insights.claim: LPU networking is compiler-scheduled with each chip acting as both processor and router, with no hardware flow control or virtual channels — thousands of chips act as one massive LPU core with minimal packet overhead.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Determinism extends to the fabric — this cuts networking silicon/cost out of scale-up interconnect, a structural cost advantage over switch-heavy GPU fabrics.
insights.quote: there is no hardware flow control or virtual channels here. Groq keeps things very bare and basic.

insights.claim: Because LPX power draw is deterministic, the rack uses look-ahead power smoothing — ordering current from regulators ahead of need — cutting voltage droop by 60% and reducing overshoot; the technique drew applause from the Hot Chips audience.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Deterministic power flattening addresses the grid/power-delivery pain point of AI datacenters — relevant to power-infrastructure suppliers and to LPX's TCO pitch versus spiky GPU loads.
insights.quote: The net effect is that it cuts down on both droop (60%) and overshoot, flattening out the overall curve.
insights.locator: The emphasis on determinism also means

insights.claim: Deterministic execution also lets the LPX software pre-plan workload placement across the chip to avoid thermal hot spots and thermal throttling.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Predictable thermals mean sustained clocks and simpler cooling — another quiet TCO edge for deterministic ASICs over GPUs in dense racks.
insights.locator: The software backing the LPX also

insights.claim: NVIDIA bridges the LPUs' synchronous domain to asynchronous GPUs and external KV cache using an FPGA as an async bridge, and must statically schedule dynamic workloads across mixed clusters.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous sync/async integration is nontrivial glue — an FPGA in the datapath signals both an interim solution and a niche FPGA design win; expect this to be integrated into silicon later.
insights.quote: So NVIDIA employs a FPGA to function as an async bridge between the two worlds.
insights.locator: Getting the LPUs and GPUs talking

insights.claim: NVIDIA disaggregates inference across silicon types: prefill runs on GPUs, most decode runs on LPUs, attention within decode is offloaded back to GPUs, and LPU/GPU racks keep separate KV caches exchanging only draft tokens (speculative decode), with micro-batching to overlap compute and communication.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Inference is fragmenting into stage-specific silicon — a template competitors (AMD, hyperscaler ASICs) must match, and a lock-in mechanism since the orchestration lives in NVIDIA's stack.
insights.quote: Only draft tokens are exchanged between the two racks.

insights.claim: NVIDIA is adding LPU support to CUDA, making Groq-derived LPUs a fully supported CUDA target, and is building LPX on the standardized MGX rack architecture for mass production and reliability.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Folding LPUs into CUDA and MGX extends NVIDIA's software moat over a formerly rival architecture — the ecosystem, not the chip, stays the durable advantage.
insights.quote: NVIDIA has adding LPU support to CUDA ecosystem, making them a fully-supported target for CUDA.
